paragraphs: Annotating a 3D object requires reconciling what different views reveal about its shape and identity. Occlusion can hide important features, and descriptions from separate viewpoints can disagree. Tri-MARF addresses these difficulties by combining images from multiple views, text descriptions, and 3D point clouds within a framework of three collaborating agents.

Each agent handles a different part of the annotation process. A vision-language agent produces descriptions from the images. An aggregation agent selects the most suitable descriptions, while a gating agent aligns the selected language with the object's 3D geometry. This division connects visual description, information selection, and geometric checking to produce more refined captions.

Experiments on Objaverse-LVIS, Objaverse-XL, and ABO report stronger performance than the compared methods. The framework reaches a CLIPScore of 88.7, against 78.6–82.4 for other state-of-the-art approaches, and processes 12,000 objects per hour on one NVIDIA A100 GPU. These findings support both the annotation quality and processing efficiency of combining complementary inputs with specialized agents in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-3d-agent-a-tri-modal-multi-.tldr: Tri-MARF combines multiple views, text, and 3D geometry through three specialized agents to improve the quality and speed of 3D object annotation.

paragraphs: Tokenization determines how text becomes a sequence of vocabulary entries before a language model processes it. This paper treats that choice as an explicit optimization problem. It contrasts this formulation with Byte Pair Encoding, which builds a vocabulary through successive merges motivated by compression.

The authors prove that their optimization problem is NP-hard through a reduction from vertex cover, then introduce GreedTok, a polynomial-time greedy algorithm. They also connect a relaxed version of the problem to weighted maximum coverage. That relaxed problem has a greedy algorithm, GreedWMC, with a known approximation guarantee. The guarantee belongs to the relaxed coverage problem; the abstract does not assign it directly to GreedTok.

On real-world text collections, GreedTok achieves better compression than BPE and Unigram, while obtaining coverage scores comparable to GreedWMC. The authors also pretrain two billion-parameter transformer language models to compare GreedTok with BPE. GreedTok produces lower bits per byte when controlling either the proportion of the dataset used or the number of training tokens, connecting its tokenization improvements to the evaluated language models.
neurips-2025-a-partition-cover-approach-.tldr: GreedTok turns tokenization into a coverage-oriented optimization problem and improves compression and language-model bits per byte in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Unfolding networks turn the steps of an iterative algorithm into an interpretable neural network. They incorporate knowledge about data structure and can reconstruct information from incomplete or noisy measurements. This paper asks how well a particular family of these networks generalizes when inputs are deliberately perturbed.

The analysis focuses on overparameterized unfolding networks and attacks generated by the fast gradient sign method under an l2-norm constraint. The authors develop a framework for estimating adversarial Rademacher complexity, a quantity used to analyze generalization under attack. From that estimate, they derive error bounds whose dependence on the attack level is tight. These are theoretical results for the studied network family and attack setting.

Experiments on real-world data corroborate the theoretical analysis across the data examined. The authors also observe that the family's extra parameters can be used to improve adversarial robustness. This connects a design choice often discussed in terms of model capacity to resistance against perturbations, offering guidance on how these structured networks might be made more robust.
neurips-2025-adversarial-generalization-.tldr: The paper derives attack-sensitive generalization bounds for a family of unfolding networks and finds that their overparameterization can support robustness.

paragraphs: Clustering asks a model to discover groups in data without being given group labels. This paper studies whether an attention mechanism can learn such structure in a mathematically specified setting. The data comes from a Gaussian mixture model, where the underlying groups have distinct centers that the learning procedure aims to recover.

The authors analyze a simplified attention layer with two heads. They define a population risk: an objective expressed over the underlying data distribution. Their result shows that minimizing this objective using unlabeled data drives the attention-head parameters toward alignment with the true mixture centroids. The learned parameters therefore acquire a direct relationship to the structure that generated the observations.

The contribution is a theoretical explanation of how attention can support unsupervised learning. It identifies both a suitable objective and the meaningful structure that optimizing it produces. Its scope is the specified Gaussian-mixture setting and simplified attention architecture, providing a concrete account of clustering behavior within that setting rather than an unrestricted claim about all transformers.
neurips-2025-attention-based-clustering-.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows that minimizing a suitable unlabeled-data objective aligns a simplified two-head attention layer with Gaussian-mixture centers.

paragraphs: A higher mathematical answer score does not reveal which reasoning abilities improved during training. SPARKLE examines reinforcement learning through three more specific dimensions: following and executing plans, incorporating supplied knowledge, and working through chains of subproblems. This makes it possible to distinguish different behavioral changes behind overall accuracy.

The analysis finds that explicit human-written plans can reduce performance on the hardest benchmarks. Reinforcement-learning-tuned models experience smaller drops than base or supervised-fine-tuned models. The authors interpret this as suggesting that reinforcement learning may strengthen internally developed strategies more than execution of externally supplied plans. Separately, they observe consistent improvements in models' ability to use provided knowledge across diverse tasks.

The paper also investigates how to reuse difficult problems that provide no reinforcement-learning signal and contain mixed-quality reasoning traces. Its SparkleRL-PSS pipeline supplies partial steps across multiple training stages to guide exploration without generating additional data. Together, the analysis and training approach connect finer-grained observations about reasoning behavior to a practical way of making difficult training material useful.
neurips-2025-beyond-accuracy-dissecting-.tldr: SPARKLE analyzes how reinforcement learning changes mathematical reasoning and introduces partial-step scaffolding to reuse difficult training problems.

paragraphs: A guardrail that detects unsafe text does not by itself determine how a language model should revise its output. C-SafeGen addresses generation directly through Claim-based Stream Decoding. As a model produces successive claims, a streaming guardrail evaluates them, and a backtracking mechanism revises claims identified as carrying high safety risk.

The paper combines this decoding procedure with statistical certification based on conformal analysis. It proves that the procedure achieves the desired generation distribution subject to safety constraints and derives a high-probability upper bound on generation risk. These guarantees concern a constrained distribution and quantified risk; they do not amount to a statement that every output is certainly safe.

The authors also extend the framework to sequentially arriving user queries, proving asymptotic control of safety risk to a chosen level. Empirical comparisons report effective and efficient decoding against state-of-the-art safety approaches. Evaluations with realistic data in offline and online settings additionally support the soundness and tightness of the risk bound, connecting the theoretical certification to observed behavior.
neurips-2025-c-safegen-certified-safe-ll.tldr: C-SafeGen revises risky claims during generation and supplies statistical risk bounds, including asymptotic risk control for online queries.

paragraphs: Driving situations can admit multiple plausible future behaviors, making a single rigid prediction difficult to use reliably. DiffE2E addresses this through a hybrid policy that combines diffusion with regression and classification. It first aligns perception features from multiple sensors at several scales using hierarchical bidirectional cross-attention.

A transformer decoder then divides the modeling work among complementary components. Diffusion represents the multiple possible future trajectories, while regression and classification explicitly model key control variables such as velocity. These components train collaboratively within a structured latent representation. A separate module integrates high-level goals with perception features, and cross-attention connects that combined information to the hybrid latent variables.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on CARLA closed-loop benchmarks and NAVSIM evaluations. Those results support combining a flexible representation of possible trajectories with more explicit control-variable predictions in the tested driving tasks. The authors also present the framework as a potentially broader approach to hybrid action representation, with extension to embodied intelligence described as a possibility rather than an established experimental result.
neurips-2025-diffe2e-rethinking-end-to-e.tldr: DiffE2E combines diffusion-based trajectory modeling with explicit control predictions and reports state-of-the-art results on two autonomous-driving evaluations.

paragraphs: A fluent summary can still omit information that matters. Conformal Importance Summarization addresses this problem by making coverage of critical content a controllable objective. The framework produces extractive summaries, selecting sentences from a document, and uses conformal prediction to provide distribution-free guarantees about the information retained.

The method calibrates thresholds on sentence-level importance scores using a small calibration set. Users specify coverage and recall rates for critical content, and the calibrated thresholds guide sentence selection. Because the framework is model-agnostic and works with black-box language models, its coverage mechanism can be combined with existing systems without requiring access to their internal parameters.

Experiments on established summarization benchmarks achieve the information coverage rate assured by the theory. This supports the specific goal of preserving important content at a controlled rate, which is especially relevant when omissions carry consequences. The authors suggest combining the method with other summarization techniques to build more reliable systems; the stated guarantees concern coverage, rather than every possible aspect of summary quality.
neurips-2025-document-summarization-with.tldr: Conformal Importance Summarization calibrates sentence selection to provide user-controlled statistical coverage guarantees for critical content.

paragraphs: Abstract visual reasoning requires finding hidden patterns and inferring the rules that connect visual examples. DSRF addresses two difficulties identified in existing approaches: deeper models can overfit, and fixed networks can struggle to accommodate different rules. Its design expands the range of reasoning pathways and adjusts processing to individual samples.

The Multi-View Reasoning Pyramid organizes features around different combinations of attributes. This widens the network's coverage of possible rule combinations while retaining layered reasoning within each view. A Dynamic Domain-Contrast Prediction block then models relationships that vary across tasks. It uses a Gram matrix to represent feature distributions and a gate matrix to capture differences between context and target features.

The two components address complementary needs: representing a wider variety of patterns and adapting comparisons to the current problem. Experiments across six abstract visual reasoning tasks report state-of-the-art performance under multiple settings. These results support the framework's combination of broader attribute coverage and sample-dependent reasoning in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-dsrf-a-dynamic-and-scalable.tldr: DSRF improves abstract visual reasoning by expanding attribute-combination pathways and dynamically adapting relationships to each problem.

paragraphs: This paper treats language-model realignment as something that can be adjusted quantitatively during both training and inference. Its training method, TrRa, combines the output scores, or logits, of a reference model and an already aligned model. Controlling that combination provides a way to steer the degree of realignment.

For inference, the authors introduce InRa, which uses a layer adapter initialized as an identity transformation near the bottom of the network. Input embeddings are processed through the adapter and original-layer pathways, with their resulting logits combined through controllable interpolation. This supplies an inference-time mechanism for adjusting behavior after training.

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, TrRa reduces token usage by 54.63% without reported performance degradation, compared with 33.86% for DeepScaleR-1.5B. The authors also adapt the 7B model to support both fast and slow thinking, and report that encouraging deeper reasoning can exceed its original performance. These examples illustrate adjustable reasoning behavior and efficiency in the studied models, with control available at more than one stage.
neurips-2025-flexible-realignment-of-lan.tldr: The framework uses controllable logit fusion and an inference adapter to adjust model behavior, demonstrating token savings and flexible reasoning depth.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a 3D face from a few images requires recovering geometry from limited visual evidence. Existing morphable-model approaches restrict that geometry through fixed shape priors, while optimization methods can be computationally expensive. GLVD combines learned reconstruction with optimization to pursue expressive face geometry at lower inference cost.

The method extends Learned Vertex Descent by optimizing a neural field for individual mesh vertices while using dynamically predicted 3D keypoints as global structural guidance. These ingredients connect local vertex adjustments to the overall arrangement of the face. Relative spatial encoding supports iterative refinement, and the method does not require dense 3D supervision.

The reported evaluations place GLVD at the state of the art for single-view reconstruction and describe it as highly competitive when multiple views are available. Inference time is also substantially reduced. The findings support the value of combining local geometric refinement with global guidance, while preserving the distinction between the strongest reported result in single-view settings and the competitive performance in multi-view settings.
neurips-2025-glvd-guided-learned-vertex-.tldr: GLVD combines per-vertex optimization with predicted 3D keypoint guidance for fast, expressive face reconstruction without dense 3D supervision.

paragraphs: Inverse problems involve reconstructing underlying information from observations, and pretrained denoisers have become useful components of reconstruction algorithms. A common approach inserts a denoiser into an iterative procedure intended to perform maximum a posteriori estimation. The difficulty is that the required mathematical operation, the proximal operator of the negative log-prior, is usually intractable.

Practitioners often substitute a denoiser for this operator without a general justification. The paper analyzes a simple algorithm closely related to practical methods and proves that it converges to the desired proximal operator when the prior is log-concave. The result therefore establishes a conditional theoretical connection between denoising models and the optimization step they are used to approximate.

The authors also interpret the algorithm as gradient descent on smoothed proximal objectives. This interpretation explains the iterative procedure through an explicit optimization framework. Its significance is a foundation for a class of previously heuristic methods, with the log-concavity assumption central to the stated guarantee rather than a claim that any denoiser substitution is valid.
neurips-2025-map-estimation-with-denoise.tldr: Under a log-concave prior, a denoiser-related iterative algorithm provably converges to the proximal operator needed for MAP optimization.

paragraphs: In single-positive multi-label learning, an example has one confirmed label even though several classes may be present. The remaining classes are unknown, so an absent annotation cannot simply be treated as evidence of absence. This setting matters when fully labeling every example would require substantial annotation effort.

The L48 dataset brings this problem into a real-world, fine-grained domain using bird-sound recordings. Earlier benchmarks commonly simulated partial labeling by randomly retaining one positive label from fully annotated datasets. L48 instead supplies a natural single-positive setting, together with two extensions where domain knowledge provides additional negative labels. These settings let researchers study different amounts of available label information.

When existing methods are evaluated on L48, their performance differs significantly from results on synthetic benchmarks. The authors also analyze weaknesses exposed by the dataset. The contribution is therefore both a new evaluation resource and evidence that synthetic label removal can miss important difficulties encountered in real partially labeled data, particularly when distinctions between classes are fine-grained.
neurips-2025-merlin-l48-spectrogram-data.tldr: L48 uses bird-sound data to benchmark naturally incomplete labels, revealing method behavior that differs from synthetic partial-label benchmarks.

paragraphs: MMAR evaluates reasoning about audio across speech, music, other sounds, and combinations of these sources. It contains 1,000 audio-question-answer examples drawn from real-world internet videos and refined through repeated corrections and quality checks. The questions require multiple reasoning steps beyond recognizing a sound or describing an immediately apparent event.

Each question is organized within a hierarchy of four reasoning layers: signal, perception, semantics, and culture. Additional subcategories capture differences in task type and complexity. Every example also includes a chain-of-thought rationale. Some questions require graduate-level perceptual or specialized domain knowledge, making the benchmark demanding along both reasoning and knowledge dimensions.

The authors evaluate a broad range of audio, multimodal, language, and reasoning models, including evaluations with audio-caption inputs. Their results and analysis identify shortcomings in current understanding and reasoning capabilities. MMAR consequently offers a structured way to examine challenging audio reasoning across domains, while its mixed audio scenarios broaden evaluation beyond benchmarks restricted to speech, music, or sound alone.
neurips-2025-mmar-a-challenging-benchmar.tldr: MMAR provides 1,000 curated, multi-step audio reasoning questions that expose limitations across a broad range of evaluated models.

paragraphs: Developing reasoning abilities across many subjects requires challenging questions beyond the familiar domains of mathematics and coding. NaturalReasoning addresses the shortage of diverse training material with a scalable question-generation approach. The resulting dataset contains 2.8 million questions and reference answers covering fields such as physics, computer science, economics, and social sciences.

The authors test the dataset through knowledge distillation, where a strong teacher model supplies reasoning capabilities that another model is trained to acquire. Their experiments show that NaturalReasoning questions can elicit those capabilities from the teacher and support their transfer. This evaluates the questions as useful training inputs, rather than treating dataset size alone as evidence of value.

The paper also demonstrates effectiveness for unsupervised self-training using either external reward models or self-rewarding. These results establish two uses for the resource: transferring reasoning from a stronger model and supporting self-training with feedback. The broader contribution is a supply of challenging questions across subject areas that can support the studied approaches to expanding reasoning capability.
neurips-2025-naturalreasoning-reasoning-.tldr: NaturalReasoning supplies 2.8 million diverse questions and demonstrates their usefulness for reasoning distillation and reward-guided self-training.

paragraphs: A 3D semantic scene graph represents both the objects in a scene and the relationships between them. This paper investigates the quality of the object features feeding that prediction process. Its analysis finds that these features strongly influence overall accuracy, highlighting a weakness in approaches that rely heavily on graph neural networks despite insufficiently discriminative inputs.

The authors develop an object encoder and pretrain it contrastively, separating object representation learning from scene graph prediction. The goal is to make object features more informative before they enter the larger prediction system. They find that this improves object classification and directly benefits relationship prediction. Inserting the pretrained encoder into existing frameworks improves all evaluated metrics.

The method additionally combines geometric and semantic information when predicting relationships, making fuller use of both kinds of evidence. Experiments on the 3DSSG dataset report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods. The results connect stronger object representations to better scene-level understanding and show that improving an input component can benefit existing prediction frameworks.
neurips-2025-object-centric-representati.tldr: Contrastively pretrained object features improve both object and relationship prediction in 3D scene graphs, including when inserted into existing frameworks.

paragraphs: Omni-Mol aims to bring diverse small-molecule tasks into one multimodal language-model framework. The paper identifies obstacles beyond limited training data: tasks can compete during joint learning, their distributions can differ substantially, and their representations may require different amounts of capacity. A shared model must accommodate these differences while learning useful common structure.

The authors organize tasks into molecule-to-molecule, molecule-to-text, molecule-to-number, and text-to-molecule categories. They assemble more than 1.4 million samples spanning over 16 tasks. The model builds on chemical knowledge available through language-model pretraining and introduces MoGE, a mixture-of-experts architecture that dynamically adjusts to the intrinsic rank required by different tasks.

Unified instruction tuning covers 16 tasks, with state-of-the-art performance reported on 13. Additional experiments support the model's scalability and versatility. These findings show that a shared framework can handle both molecular generation and understanding across the evaluated tasks, while the adaptive architecture directly addresses the differing representation needs that make joint molecular learning difficult.
neurips-2025-omni-mol-multitask-molecula.tldr: Omni-Mol combines a large molecular instruction dataset with task-adaptive experts, achieving state-of-the-art results on 13 of 16 jointly tuned tasks.

paragraphs: Models for graphs, sets, and point clouds often accept inputs of different sizes, but that architectural flexibility does not by itself establish that learned performance transfers across sizes. This paper develops a general mathematical framework for studying such transfer, extending a line of work previously explored for graph neural networks.

The central result characterizes transferability precisely as continuity in an appropriate limit space. That space is built by identifying smaller problem instances with equivalent larger ones, using equivalences determined by the data and learning task. In this formulation, the relationship between instances of different sizes becomes part of the mathematical definition of successful transfer.

The authors apply the framework to existing architectures and implement changes needed to ensure transferability within it. They also derive principles for constructing new transferable models, with numerical experiments supporting the findings. The contribution links an abstract characterization to concrete architectural design: reasoning about size generalization requires specifying how problems correspond across dimensions, then making the model behave continuously under that correspondence.
neurips-2025-on-transferring-transferabi.tldr: The paper characterizes size transferability through continuity in a task-dependent limit space and uses that framework to guide model design.

paragraphs: Forecasting a physical system becomes difficult when observations reveal only part of its state and earlier events continue to influence its evolution. Solar dynamics illustrates this problem: visible surface and atmospheric measurements leave internal processes unobserved. This paper studies probabilistic prediction for such partially observable systems with long temporal memory.

The authors identify inadequate use of historical information as a major reason standard inference procedures, including autoregressive rollouts, miss long-range dependencies. Their alternative is a multiscale inference scheme for diffusion models. It represents trajectories at fine temporal resolution near the present and at progressively coarser resolution farther away, allowing a longer temporal span to be represented without increasing computational cost.

When incorporated into a diffusion model, this scheme reduces bias in predicted distributions and improves rollout stability. These findings concern both the distribution of possible futures and the behavior of predictions over time. The contribution shows how changing the temporal organization of inference can help a forecasting model use long-range information more effectively in the studied physical setting.
neurips-2025-predicting-partially-observ.tldr: A multiscale diffusion inference scheme captures longer temporal dependencies without extra computational cost, reducing forecast bias and improving rollout stability.

paragraphs: Referring expression segmentation identifies the image region described by a user's words. RESAnything broadens the expressions it can handle to include object parts and indirect references involving function, material, style, or design. These queries require connecting descriptive properties to a region even when the wording does not name the object or part directly.

A foundational segmentation model first supplies candidate regions. Through systematic attribute prompting, a language model generates detailed descriptions involving properties such as shape, color, and location. Chain-of-thought reasoning connects these attributes to the user's expression. The approach operates in an open-vocabulary, zero-shot setting without requiring part annotations for training or fine-tuning.

The authors report stronger performance than other zero-shot methods on traditional referring-segmentation benchmarks, along with substantial gains in challenging implicit-query and part-relation scenarios. They also introduce approximately 3,000 curated benchmark instances for evaluating arbitrary, part-level references. Together, the method and dataset address the gap between recognizing named regions and interpreting richer descriptions of what a region is like or what it does.
neurips-2025-resanything-attribute-promp.tldr: RESAnything uses attribute descriptions and language-model reasoning to segment objects and parts from explicit or implicit references without part-specific training.

paragraphs: Turning a table image into usable LaTeX requires recovering both its content and its organization. Large tables, nested structures, and irregular cell contents make this especially difficult. This paper analyzes those challenges and weaknesses in existing evaluation protocols before developing a multimodal language-model approach to table reconstruction.

The method first fine-tunes a pretrained model on a large table-to-LaTeX dataset. It then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization with two rewards: one evaluates the structure of the generated LaTeX, while the other measures the appearance of its rendered output. This connects training to the final visual result as well as to the code that produces it.

Evaluation likewise combines structural and visual measurements through TEDS-Structure and CW-SSIM. The authors report state-of-the-art performance, especially for structurally complex tables. The findings support using both kinds of feedback when the desired output is executable document code: producing plausible text is only part of the task, because that text must also render into a faithful reconstruction.
neurips-2025-table2latex-rl-high-fidelit.tldr: Table2LaTeX-RL rewards both code structure and rendered appearance to improve table-image reconstruction, especially for complex layouts.

paragraphs: A reasoning model can access a code interpreter yet still use it inefficiently. The paper identifies friction between the model's probabilistic internal reasoning and the interpreter's deterministic results, which can lead to unproductive deliberation. CoRT is a post-training framework designed to teach models how to coordinate these two forms of computation.

Its Hint-Engineering strategy inserts varied hints at selected points in reasoning paths to create examples that integrate code use with thinking. The authors synthesize 30 high-quality samples for supervised fine-tuning of models ranging from 1.5B to 32B parameters. Rejection sampling and reinforcement learning further refine the alternation between internal reasoning and repeated interpreter calls.

Across five mathematical reasoning datasets, CoRT yields absolute improvements of 4% for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B and 8% for its 1.5B counterpart. Relative to pure natural-language reasoning baselines, token use falls by approximately 30% and 50%, respectively. These results support training tool coordination as a reasoning skill, with gains in both accuracy and efficiency for the evaluated models.
neurips-2025-teaching-language-models-to.tldr: CoRT trains reasoning models to interleave thinking with code-interpreter use, improving mathematical results while reducing token consumption.

paragraphs: Classifier-free guidance improves diffusion generation and alignment with input conditions, but it requires particular training procedures and applies to conditional generation. Token Perturbation Guidance aims to make similar guidance benefits available without those requirements. It operates on intermediate token representations inside the diffusion network.

The method applies perturbation matrices through a norm-preserving shuffle to produce a stable guidance signal. It requires neither additional training nor architectural changes and can be used for both conditional and unconditional generation. The authors also analyze its guidance term, finding that its effect on sampling resembles classifier-free guidance more closely than existing training-free alternatives do.

Evaluations on SDXL and Stable Diffusion 2.1 support its practical usefulness. For unconditional generation, the paper reports nearly a twofold improvement in FID over the SDXL baseline, while prompt alignment closely matches classifier-free guidance. These results connect the proposed internal perturbations to improved generation quality and indicate a route to guidance when conditioning information or specialized guidance training is unavailable.
neurips-2025-token-perturbation-guidance.tldr: Token Perturbation Guidance uses training-free internal shuffling to improve conditional and unconditional diffusion generation without changing the architecture.

paragraphs: This paper studies transformer learning in a controlled setting: predicting random walks on circles. The purpose is to explain both what a trained transformer can achieve and how its components implement the prediction. Under the analyzed conditions, a one-layer transformer trained by gradient descent reaches optimal predictive accuracy.

The theoretical account assigns distinct roles to attention and the value matrix. Softmax attention selects the direct parent state relevant to the next prediction. The value matrix then applies a one-step probability transition from that state. This gives an interpretable description of the learned computation, connecting the network's operations to the statistical process it predicts.

The authors also identify edge cases outside their theory where learning actually fails, supporting the tightness of the theoretical conditions. Their investigation further shows that small initialization can cause gradient descent to fail or struggle on some simple tasks beyond random walks. Experiments support the analysis, making both successful learning and its boundary conditions part of the paper's explanation.
neurips-2025-towards-understanding-trans.tldr: Under specified conditions, a one-layer transformer learns optimal random-walk prediction through interpretable state selection and transition operations.

paragraphs: Visibility reconstruction asks for a polygon whose visibility relationships match a supplied graph. This is difficult because small changes in vertex positions can substantially change those relationships. VisDiff tackles the problem with a diffusion model that uses an intermediate geometric representation instead of predicting the polygon's vertices directly.

The model first estimates the polygon's signed distance function, then extracts vertex locations from it. The authors find that this route learns visibility relationships more effectively than direct vertex generation. They construct a curated training and evaluation dataset and report a 26% improvement in F1 score over standard and state-of-the-art comparison methods.

The paper also presents preliminary results for visibility-graph recognition, where the supplied graph may not correspond to any polygon. It extends the approach to triangulation graphs and demonstrates diverse polygon sampling, including interpolation between polygons and between graphs. These additional results explore the representation's reach beyond reconstruction, while the recognition findings remain explicitly preliminary. The central contribution is evidence that an intermediate distance-based representation helps learn a sensitive combinatorial structure.
neurips-2025-visdiff-sdf-guided-polygon-.tldr: VisDiff reconstructs polygons from visibility graphs through signed distance functions, improving F1 and enabling diverse geometric sampling.
